lessons.title: How to search smart
objectives: Explain how a search engine finds and ranks results
Use advanced search techniques to refine results
Evaluate the reliability of a source

keywords.def: software that searches an index of web pages for matching results
a huge list of web pages built by crawling the web
a set of rules used to rank search results
a one-sided view that is unfair or not balanced

starter: Bismillah. Name two search engines you or your family use.
What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
How do you decide which search result to click on?

teach.heading: How search engines work
bullets: Crawlers follow links and visit pages.
Pages are stored in an index.
An algorithm ranks results for your query.
teach.note: Explain in three stages: crawl, index, rank. Search engines do not search the live web when you press enter; they search their index. Misconception: the first result is the 'best' or 'truest'. Ranking depends on many factors including relevance, links and paid adverts.

teach.heading: Smarter searches
bullets: Use quotation marks for an exact phrase.
Use minus to exclude a word.
Use site: to search one website.
Use filters for date and type.
teach.note: Demonstrate each technique live with real examples such as searching for "Ibn al-Haytham" optics, then adding site:bbc.co.uk. Discuss how the number of results changes. Different search engines may behave differently, so tell pupils to check the help page.

teach.heading: Adverts and ranking
bullets: Some top results are paid adverts.
teach.note: Show a results page and ask pupils to spot adverts. Discuss who benefits when you click an advert. Ask: why might a company pay to be at the top?

teach.heading: Evaluating sources
bullets: Date: is it up to date?
Purpose: to inform or to sell?
teach.note: Compare two pages on the same topic. Relate to the Islamic emphasis on verifying news before spreading it (Surah al-Hujurat 49:6 urges believers to verify news brought by a wrongdoer before acting). Use this as an ethos link to checking sources carefully.

practice: Which search finds the exact phrase 'solar system'? ("solar system" in quotation marks)
How would you search for jaguar the animal but not the car? (jaguar -car)
Give two clues that a web page is not reliable.
independent: Research 'How many people live in Cairo?' using three different websites and record the answers and sources in a table.
Rate each source for author, date, evidence and purpose out of 4 and decide which is most reliable.
Write a short paragraph explaining how you would teach a Year 6 pupil to search smart.
exit: Name the three stages of how a search engine works.
Give one search technique and explain what it does.
lessons.homework: Find a news story shared on social media and check it using two other reliable sources. Report whether it was accurate.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a search-technique card with examples and a checklist with icons for evaluating sources. Stretch: investigate how search engines may personalise results and why that matters.

lessons.title: Copyright and Copywrongs
objectives: Explain what copyright is and why it exists
Describe how to use other people's work legally
Identify examples of copyright infringement

keywords.def: the legal right of a creator to control how their work is used
breaking copyright law by using work without permission
official permission to use something under stated conditions
copying someone's work and pretending it is yours

starter: Bismillah. How would you feel if someone copied your homework and handed it in as theirs?
Name something creative that someone has made (a book, a photo, an app).
Can you save any picture from the internet and use it as your own?

teach.heading: What is copyright?
bullets: In the UK it is the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
teach.note: State that copyright arises automatically when original work is created; no symbol is needed. Copyright lasts for a long time (for most works, the life of the creator plus 70 years in the UK); you may mention this as a general rule. Ask why creators deserve protection for their time and skill.

teach.heading: Breaking the law
bullets: Copying and sharing films or e-books illegally.
teach.note: Give realistic examples for pupils: downloading a film from an unofficial website, or using a photo from a search result on a poster. Penalties can include fines. Misconception: 'if it is on the internet it is free to use'.

teach.heading: Using work legally
bullets: Use Creative Commons or public domain work.
teach.note: Show a Creative Commons image search and explain licence conditions such as attribution. Show how to write a reference. Link to honesty and amanah: giving credit and not taking what is not ours is part of our trustworthiness.

teach.heading: Plagiarism
bullets: Copy and paste is not research.
teach.note: Compare an original paragraph with a copied version and a rewritten version. Discuss how schools and exam boards treat plagiarism seriously. Show how to reference a website by title, site and date accessed.

practice: Is this legal? Downloading a new film from a free website that is not an official service.
A pupil uses a photo from a search on a school poster without asking. What should they do?
Give two ways to use another person's work legally.
independent: Create a leaflet 'Copyright facts for Year 7' with five key points.
Find an image you can legally use under a Creative Commons licence and write the correct credit.
Rewrite a short paragraph from a website in your own words and add a reference.
lessons.homework: Find out what the Creative Commons 'attribution' licence requires you to do. Write two sentences explaining it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sorting task (legal / not legal) with pictures and key words. Stretch: debate whether copyright laws are fair when someone cannot afford to buy a book or an app.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Binary, safety and Boolean logic
lessons.title: Staying safe online: risks, cyber abuse and keeping evidence
lessons.bigQuestion: If someone sends you something hurtful in a group chat and then deletes it, has it really gone?
objectives: To understand how to protect our accounts and respond to cyber abuse safely and lawfully
successCriteria: All: name three online risks and one way to protect against each
Most: describe how to collect evidence and report cyber abuse
Some: explain how UK law and Islamic teaching both protect people from online abuse
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: the Malicious Communications Act 1988 and the Protection from Harassment Act 1997
lessons.smsc: Moral: safety of others from our words and actions online

keywords.def: a fake message that tricks you into giving private information
logging in with two proofs, such as a password and a code
using technology to threaten, harass or humiliate someone
proof such as screenshots, dates and usernames

hook.text: If someone sends you something hurtful in a group chat and then deletes it, has it really gone?
hook.a: Others may have seen, saved or screenshotted it; and you can keep evidence too before it is deleted.

islamicLink.text: Allah forbids mocking others and calling them offensive names (al-Hujurat 49:11) and forbids spying and backbiting (al-Hujurat 49:12). The Prophet ﷺ said that a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Our keyboards are part of our hands and tongues.

starter.q: What is a strong password made from?
starter.a: Three random words, ideally with numbers or symbols.
Information that identifies you, such as your address or date of birth.

starter.q: Name one sign that a message might be fake.
starter.a: Urgency, a strange link, spelling mistakes or a request for a password.

starter.q: Who can you tell if something online worries you?
starter.a: A parent, a teacher or the school's safeguarding lead.

teach.heading: Risks and protections
bullets: Weak passwords: use three random words
teach.note: Calm, practical tone. School staff never ask for passwords; never post one in Teams chat.

head: Risk
Protection
rows: Check the sender; never type a password from a link
Strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication
First name only; no address, school or location
Do not accept or reply; tell an adult

teach.heading: Teams and portal behaviour
bullets: Chat is for learning, kept by the school
Leave and tell if something feels wrong
teach.note: TGA rule: camera background plain, first name, stay on the lesson window. Recording or screenshotting others is not allowed.

teach.heading: Cyber abuse
teach.note: Use fictional examples only. Some pupils may have experienced this: it is never the victim's fault.

teach.heading: Evidence and reporting
bullets: Screenshot: message, username, date and time
Block and report on the platform
teach.note: In the UK, harassment and threatening messages can be crimes. CEOP and Childline (0800 1111) also help.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: What should a screenshot used as evidence show?
options: The message, username, date and time
check.why: Without who and when, evidence is hard to act on; replying can make things worse.

practice.q: A message: 'Your Microsoft account is locked. Log in here within 1 hour.' Name three warning signs.
practice.a: Urgency, a link to log in, an unexpected message (check the sender address too).
practice.model: Teacher underlines: '1 hour' (urgency), 'log in here' (link asking for credentials), not expected (check the real sender address).

practice.q: What is two-factor authentication?
practice.a: Logging in with two proofs, such as a password and a code from a phone.

practice.q: Order: report, do not reply, screenshot, tell, block.
practice.a: Do not reply, screenshot, block, report, tell.

independent.q: Core: Read the three scenarios. For each, write the risk, what to do and who to tell, in the portal response box.
independent.a: Each answer names the risk, uses the evidence steps and names a trusted adult.
independent.model: Teacher completes scenario 1: risk (phishing), action (do not click, report), tell (parent and teacher).

independent.q: Extend: Write a paragraph: how does UK law protect people from online abuse? Start: 'In the UK, sending threatening messages...'
independent.a: In the UK, sending threatening or grossly offensive messages can be an offence (Malicious Communications Act 1988), and repeated harassment is a crime (Protection from Harassment Act 1997).

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how Islamic teaching on speech and the evidence steps work together.
independent.a: Islam forbids harming others with words; the steps stop the harm, protect the victim and let adults act justly.

exit.q: Two-factor authentication uses... A) two passwords B) a password and a second proof such as a code C) two usernames
exit.a: B) a password and a second proof such as a code
options: A password and a second proof

exit.q: Big question: if a hurtful message is deleted, has it really gone? Why does it matter for evidence?
exit.a: Not necessarily: others may have saved it; screenshot quickly so adults can act.

lessons.homework: With a parent, turn on two-factor authentication or check privacy settings on one account you use (school or family).
lessons.send: SEND: scenario cards with the steps printed. EAL: evidence, report, harassment glossary. Stretch: compare reporting tools on two platforms.

lessons.title: Cyber abuse and keeping evidence
objectives: Describe different forms of cyber abuse and their impact
Explain how to collect evidence and report abuse
Understand relevant UK law and our responsibilities

keywords.def: using technology to repeatedly hurt, threaten or embarrass someone
proof such as screenshots, dates and usernames
stop a person from contacting you on an app
a person who helps or speaks up when someone is being bullied

starter: Bismillah. What is a digital footprint?
Why can online unkindness hurt more than unkindness in person?
Who are the trusted adults you can go to for help?

teach.heading: What is cyber abuse?
teach.note: Use fictional examples only. Be sensitive: some pupils may have experienced this. Explain that it can happen 24 hours a day, can be seen by many people and can be hard to remove. Explain the impact on mental health and trust.

teach.heading: Our values
bullets: Allah forbids mockery and bad nicknames.
Hadith: the Muslim is the one whom people are safe from.
teach.note: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other people are safe (Bukhari and Muslim). Apply this to typing and posting: our fingers are included. Qur'an 49:11 forbids ridiculing others and giving offensive nicknames.

teach.heading: Evidence and reporting
bullets: Take screenshots with date and username.
Block and use the report button.
teach.note: Walk through collecting evidence: screenshot the messages, note the date and time, do not delete them. Show where the report tool is in an app. Reporting is not 'snitching'; it protects people. Mention that schools have anti-bullying policies and a designated safeguarding lead.

teach.heading: The law
teach.note: Keep it age-appropriate: some online messages that are threatening, grossly offensive or harassing can be criminal offences in the UK. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access to computer systems illegal. Explain that this is why we think before sending, and why we do not hack others' accounts.

practice: A group chat is mocking a classmate. List three things a good upstander could do.
Put in order: tell a trusted adult, take screenshots, block the user, do not reply.
Is it okay to log in to a friend's account as a joke if you know their password? Explain with reference to the law.
independent: Write a leaflet 'What to do if you are cyberbullied' with the evidence steps and where to get help.
Plan a role-play of how to support a friend who is being targeted online.
Write a paragraph explaining why Islamic teachings and UK law both discourage online abuse.
exit: Name two pieces of evidence you should keep if you are bullied online.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page checklist of the steps to take if you or a friend experience cyber abuse. Include who to tell and where to find support.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a visual step-by-step card with icons and a word bank; allow oral role-play. Stretch: research how a social media platform's reporting process works and evaluate it.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Binary, safety and Boolean logic
lessons.title: Binary: bits, bytes and converting numbers
lessons.bigQuestion: A light switch is either on or off. How could you count to 7 using only three switches?
objectives: To understand how computers represent numbers in binary
successCriteria: All: explain why computers use binary (on/off)
Most: convert binary numbers up to 8 bits into denary
Some: convert denary numbers up to 255 into binary
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: place value and powers of 2
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the contribution of Muslim scholars such as al-Khwarizmi to number and algorithms

keywords.def: a number system using only 0 and 1 (base 2)
one binary digit, 0 or 1
a group of 8 bits
our everyday number system with digits 0 to 9 (base 10)

hook.text: A light switch is either on or off. How could you count to 7 using only three switches?
hook.a: Give the switches values 4, 2, 1 and add the ones that are on: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.

islamicLink.text: The numbers we use every day, 0 to 9 with place value, reached Europe through Muslim scholars: al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century work on Hindu numerals helped spread them, and the word 'algorithm' comes from his name. Binary uses the same idea of place value with only two digits.

starter.q: What should evidence of cyber abuse show?
starter.a: The message, username, date and time.

starter.q: What is the value of the 3 in 352?
Name one input and one output device.

teach.heading: Why binary?
bullets: Computers are made of billions of switches (transistors)
teach.note: Everything (numbers, text, images) is stored as bits.

teach.heading: Place value in binary
teach.note: Compare with denary columns 1000, 100, 10, 1.

teach.heading: Binary to denary
teach.note: Model it.

teach.heading: Denary to binary
bullets: If it fits, write 1 and subtract
teach.note: Model 45: 32 fits (13 left), 16 no, 8 fits (5 left), 4 fits (1 left), 2 no, 1 fits: 00101101.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: 4 + 2 = 6. '110' reads the bits as a denary number, a common trap.

practice.q: Convert 00010010 to denary.
practice.model: Teacher writes place values above the bits and adds 16 and 2.

practice.q: Convert 11111111 to denary.
Convert 20 to 8-bit binary.

independent.q: Extend: Convert to 8-bit binary: 9, 37, 100, 200.
Stretch: What is the largest number one byte can store, and how many different values is that?
independent.a: 255; 256 different values (0 to 255).

exit.q: A byte is... A) 4 bits B) 8 bits C) 10 bits
exit.a: B) 8 bits

exit.q: Convert 00001111 to denary.

lessons.homework: Write your age and the day of the month you were born in 8-bit binary.
lessons.send: SEND: printed place-value grid. EAL: binary, denary, bit, byte. Stretch: binary addition 00000101 + 00000011.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Binary, safety and Boolean logic
lessons.title: Boolean logic: true, false, AND, OR, NOT
lessons.bigQuestion: 'You can join the lesson if your camera works AND your microphone works.' What if only one works?
objectives: To understand how Boolean operators combine true and false conditions
successCriteria: All: say whether a simple statement is true or false
Most: evaluate expressions with AND, OR and NOT
Some: write a Boolean condition for a real rule
lessons.crossCurricular: English: precise meaning of 'and', 'or' and 'not' in rules
lessons.smsc: Moral: rules with conditions, such as the conditions for zakah (owning the nisab for a full year)

keywords.def: a value that is either true or false
true only when both inputs are true
true when at least one input is true
reverses true and false

hook.text: 'You can join the lesson if your camera works AND your microphone works.' What if only one works?
hook.a: With AND, both must be true; one working is not enough.

starter.q: How many bits in a byte?
What does 1 mean in a computer switch?

teach.heading: True or false
teach.note: Statements: 'London is in England' (true); '5 > 9' (false).

teach.heading: AND, OR, NOT
teach.note: Real rules.

teach.heading: Evaluating expressions
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: age = 14, hasPermission = false. Evaluate (age >= 13) AND hasPermission.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: isRaining = false, isCold = true. What is isRaining OR isCold?
check.why: OR needs at least one true: isCold is true.

practice.q: Evaluate: NOT (5 > 3).
practice.a: 5 > 3 is true, so NOT true = false.
practice.model: Teacher: inside the brackets first, 5 > 3 is true; NOT flips it to false.

practice.q: Evaluate: (2 = 2) AND (3 > 7).
Evaluate: (10 < 4) OR (6 = 6).

independent.q: Core: Evaluate the 8 expressions on the worksheet.
independent.a: Answers on the teacher key; each shows the two parts and the result.

independent.q: Extend: Write a Boolean condition for: 'A pupil may join the class Team if they have a school account and their parent has signed the agreement.'
independent.a: hasSchoolAccount AND agreementSigned

independent.q: Stretch: Write a condition for 'entry is free for under 5s or over 65s, but not on event days'.
independent.a: (age < 5 OR age > 65) AND NOT eventDay

exit.q: true AND false = ? A) true B) false
exit.a: B) false

exit.q: Big question: camera works, microphone does not. Can you join with an AND rule? Why?
exit.a: No: AND needs both conditions true.

lessons.homework: Write three rules from home or school as Boolean conditions using AND, OR or NOT.
lessons.send: SEND: true/false cards (1 and 0). EAL: true, false, both, either. Stretch: De Morgan: is NOT (A AND B) the same as NOT A OR NOT B? Test it.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Binary, safety and Boolean logic
lessons.title: Logic gates and truth tables
lessons.bigQuestion: A car's interior light comes on if the driver's door OR the passenger's door is open. Which logic gate does that use?
objectives: To understand how AND, OR and NOT gates process binary inputs, shown in truth tables
successCriteria: All: recognise the symbols for AND, OR and NOT gates
Most: complete truth tables for each gate
Some: use a truth table to describe a real situation
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: series and parallel circuits behave like AND and OR
lessons.smsc: Social: safety systems built from simple logic (fire alarms, lift doors)

keywords.def: an electronic component that applies a Boolean operation
a table showing the output for every input combination
a 0 or 1 going into a gate
the 0 or 1 coming out of a gate

hook.text: A car's interior light comes on if the driver's door OR the passenger's door is open. Which logic gate does that use?
hook.a: An OR gate: either input being 1 gives an output of 1.

starter.a: Only when both inputs are true.

teach.heading: Gates in hardware
teach.note: Gates are the physical form of Boolean logic.

teach.heading: AND gate
bullets: Output 1 only if A and B are 1
teach.note: Example: a microwave runs only if door is shut AND start pressed.

teach.heading: OR gate
bullets: Output 1 if A or B (or both) is 1
teach.note: Interior car light.

teach.heading: NOT gate
teach.note: A light that is on when it is NOT daytime.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: An AND gate has inputs A = 1, B = 0. Output?
check.why: AND needs both inputs to be 1.

practice.q: Complete the AND truth table from memory.
practice.model: Teacher lists the four input rows in binary order 00, 01, 10, 11 and applies 'both must be 1'.

practice.q: Which gate: 'the alarm sounds if the window OR the door is opened'?
NOT gate input 1. Output?

independent.q: Core: Complete the truth tables for AND, OR and NOT on the worksheet and draw each symbol.
independent.a: Tables as on the slides; correct symbols.
independent.model: Teacher draws the AND symbol and fills its first row.

independent.q: Extend: Build each gate in the CircuitVerse simulator with two switches and a light. Check every row.
independent.a: Each gate's light matches its truth table.

independent.q: Stretch: A vending machine gives a drink if a coin is inserted AND a button is pressed. Write its truth table and say which gate.
independent.a: AND: output 1 only for coin 1, button 1.

exit.q: OR gate, A = 0, B = 0. Output? A) 0 B) 1
Big question: which gate does a car's interior light use, and why?
exit.a: OR: the light comes on if either door is open.

lessons.homework: Find two everyday devices that use AND or OR logic and write a truth table for one.
lessons.send: SEND: gate symbol cards with the rule written inside. EAL: input, output, gate. Stretch: research the XOR gate.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Binary, safety and Boolean logic
lessons.title: Combining gates; logic quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: A safe opens only if the right code is entered AND it is NOT night time. How many gates do you need?
objectives: To understand how logic gates combine into circuits and how to work out their output
successCriteria: All: follow inputs through a two-gate circuit
Most: complete a truth table for a combined circuit
Some: design a circuit from a written rule
lessons.smsc: Moral: security systems protecting what is entrusted to us

keywords.def: two or more gates joined together
a written form of a circuit, such as (A AND B) OR C
a value between gates, worked out first
one set of input values

hook.text: A safe opens only if the right code is entered AND it is NOT night time. How many gates do you need?
hook.a: Two: a NOT gate on 'night', then an AND gate with 'code'.

starter.q: How many rows in a two-input truth table?

teach.heading: Joining gates
bullets: The output of one gate is the input of the next
teach.note: Example: Q = NOT (A AND B).

teach.heading: Model: a combined truth table
bullets: Add a column for the middle value
teach.note: Model for Q = (A AND B) OR C, first rows.

model.problem: Q = (A AND B) OR C. Find Q when A = 1, B = 0, C = 1.

teach.heading: Three inputs, eight rows
teach.note: Truth table for Q = (A AND B) OR C.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Q = NOT (A OR B). A = 0, B = 0. Q?
check.why: A OR B = 0, then NOT 0 = 1. Doing the NOT first is the trap.

practice.q: Q = NOT A AND B. Find Q for A = 0, B = 1.
practice.model: Teacher: NOT applies to A only: NOT 0 = 1; then AND with B (1) gives 1.

practice.q: Write the expression for: 'the light is on if switch A is on and switch B is off'.

independent.q: Core: Complete the truth table for Q = NOT (A AND B) (4 rows) on the worksheet.
independent.model: Teacher completes row 00: A AND B = 0, NOT 0 = 1.

independent.q: Extend: Build Q = (A AND B) OR C in CircuitVerse and check two rows of the slide table.
independent.a: Lights match the table rows tested.

exit.q: Logic quiz (portal, 10 questions): binary conversions, Boolean expressions, gate truth tables and a combined circuit.
exit.a: Teacher marks in the portal.

exit.q: Big question: how many gates for 'code correct AND NOT night', and which?
exit.a: Two: NOT and AND.

lessons.homework: Write the Boolean expression and truth table for: 'The fan turns on if it is hot and the window is not open.'
lessons.send: SEND: truth tables with input columns filled in. EAL: expression, circuit, combination. Stretch: design a circuit for a majority vote of three switches.

lessons.title: What is a network? LAN, WAN and devices
lessons.bigQuestion: Your online lesson travels from your teacher's house to yours. What do you think it passes through on the way?
objectives: To understand what a network is, the difference between a LAN and a WAN, and the devices that connect them
successCriteria: All: define a network
Most: compare a LAN and a WAN
Some: explain the role of a router, switch and server
lessons.smsc: Social: networks connecting people and communities

keywords.def: two or more devices connected to share data
local area network: a small area such as a home
wide area network: across a large area; the internet is one
a device that sends data between networks

hook.text: Your online lesson travels from your teacher's house to yours. What do you think it passes through on the way?
hook.a: The home router, the internet service provider, many routers across the internet, and your router.

starter.q: Give one tip for a strong password (Spring 1).

head: Device
Job
rows: Provides a service, such as web pages

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: The internet is an example of a ...

practice.q: Is a school's network a LAN or WAN? Explain.
practice.a: A LAN: it covers one site and is owned by the school.
practice.model: I do: area? one building. Owner? the school. So LAN.

independent.q: Map your home network (pupil PDF): devices, router, how they connect (wired or Wi-Fi), and where the internet comes in.
independent.a: A labelled diagram of the home network.
independent.model: The teacher draws a sample home network.

independent.q: Extend: explain why a home network is a LAN but uses a WAN.
independent.a: Devices form a LAN; the router connects it to the internet (a WAN).

independent.q: Stretch: research how undersea cables carry internet traffic between continents.
independent.a: A short explanation.

exit.a: sends data between networks

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Your online lesson travels from your teacher's house to yours. What do you think it passes through on the way?
